summary: The article argues that the Los Angeles Dodgers may not pursue both Shohei Ohtani and Mike Trout in free agency, even though both could be available from the Angels. It weighs payroll limits, the Dodgers' need for pitching, Ohtani's elbow injury recovery, and Trout's injury history. It concludes that Trout may be the more logical choice because of his lower price, though he has said he wants to stay with the Angels.
one_line: An opinion piece explaining why the Dodgers may not sign both Shohei Ohtani and Mike Trout, citing payroll, injuries and pitching needs.
key_facts: Shohei Ohtani's next contract is projected at around $500–$600 million, which would break Mike Trout's record deal of 12 years, $426.5 million.
The Dodgers' lineup this season was valued at $283 million.
Trout's annual salary is about $35.45 million, and with seven years left on his Angels contract the Dodgers would owe $248.15 million plus any extension value.
Sports Illustrated predicted $535 million over 11 years for Ohtani, about $48.63 million annually.
Six Dodgers earn above $10 million a year: Freddie Freeman ($27M), Mookie Betts ($25M), Clayton Kershaw ($20M), Chris Taylor ($15M), Max Muncy ($13.5M) and J.D. Martinez ($10M).
Kershaw's exit and other offloads would free enough payroll for two $25 million or three $10 million players, which does not fit Trout or Ohtani.
Ohtani had 167 strikeouts this season and will not pitch in 2024 because of an elbow ligament injury, so signing him may be inadvisable until 2025.
Freeman and Betts had 211 and 179 hits respectively this regular season.
Trout's career totals are 1624 hits, 940 RBIs, an 85.2 WAR and a .301 BA over 12 years.
Trout has been injured since 2022, with five injuries in that season and two hand injuries in consecutive months in 2023.
The Angels won 73 games this season, which makes affording Trout in the future difficult.
Trout is 32 years old, and the article says he has about 6 more years left to give.
